questions.q: Why does the lesson say treating peer review as optional, just because there's no formal journal requiring it, is a mistake?
options: Because peer review is legally required for all student work
Because unreviewed reports are automatically rejected by all employers
It skips the step most likely to catch the gap between what you think you wrote and what you actually wrote
Because peer review always finds at least ten errors in any report
questions.explain: The lesson frames peer review as a core practice that catches exactly the gap between intended and actual writing, regardless of whether a formal journal requires it.

questions.q: What does the lesson's structured self-review pass ask you to check first, before anyone else reads your report?
options: Whether the abstract/summary's claim matches what the results section's numbers actually support, using the same reading pass from Lesson 2
Whether the report includes a dedicated marketing section
Whether the report is at least 20 pages long
Whether the report is formatted in a specific font
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly reuses Lesson 2's critical-reading pass, applied to your own writing, starting with whether the claim matches the actual supporting numbers.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend asking a reviewer specific questions ('does my methods section give enough detail to replicate this?') rather than a vague 'can you look this over?'
options: Because reviewers refuse to answer vague questions under any circumstances
Because vague requests take longer for a reviewer to read
Because specific questions are required by academic publishing standards
Vague requests tend to produce vague, unhelpful feedback; specific questions get specific, actionable answers
questions.explain: The lesson states directly that naming the specific thing you want checked produces more useful, actionable feedback than a vague request.

questions.q: What are the three feedback triage categories this lesson describes?
options: Technical, non-technical, and irrelevant
Must-fix, worth considering, and noted but not changing
Urgent, low-priority, and spam
Accepted, rejected, and pending peer review
questions.explain: The lesson defines these three triage categories explicitly, with guidance that must-fix items (factual errors, unsupported claims, unclear methods) should be addressed before finalizing.

questions.q: A reviewer points out the conclusion claims mitigation 'significantly' helps, but no significance test appears in the results section. Per this lesson's triage categories, how should this be handled?
options: As an item to discuss only if time allows after the report is already finalized
As a must-fix -- either add the significance test/results or remove the word 'significantly' so the conclusion matches what's actually shown
As a stylistic preference to note and ignore
As feedback that should be dismissed because reviewers cannot comment on statistical language
questions.explain: This is a genuine unsupported claim -- the conclusion asserts something ('significantly') the results section doesn't actually demonstrate -- which the lesson's must-fix category is specifically meant to catch before finalizing the report.
